title: Moses and the shepherd
hookLine: a shepherd prays to comb God's hair and wash God's feet, and Moses scolds him (Masnavi 2.1720ff)

cards: Listen to a small child pray at bedtime. Thank you for the dog. Please make Grandma's knee better.
Are you cold up there? Adults sometimes smile, and sometimes wince a little: that's not how you talk to God. There's a right way, isn't there?
The proper words, the ones in the book. Rumi tells a story about exactly this, in the Masnavi. It's the story this week is named for, and it takes three days.
It begins with a man alone on a hillside with his goats.

teach.b: It's in Book Two. Moses, honored as a prophet in Judaism, Christianity and Islam, is walking along a road when he hears a shepherd praying out loud, something like this. God, where are you?

teach.h: I'D COMB YOUR HAIR AND WASH YOUR FEET.
teach.b: I'd mend your shoes and comb your hair. I'd wash your clothes and pick out your lice. I'd bring you milk.
I'd kiss your little hand and rub your little feet, and sweep out the place where you sleep at night. All my goats are yours. This man has no learning.
He's offering God the only things he knows how to give: the care you'd give someone you love who's tired and far from home. Moses stops. Who are you talking to?
The shepherd says: the one who made us, and made the earth and sky. Moses is horrified.
In Rumi's telling, he tells the shepherd he's talking nonsense, that he should stuff cotton in his mouth, that God has no need of shoes and socks and milk.
Talk like that, Moses says, is fit for a body that grows and needs feeding, not for God. Moses isn't wrong about God; Rumi's tradition teaches that God has no body. But watch what the scolding does.
The shepherd says, you've shut my mouth and set my soul on fire with regret. He tears his clothes, lets out a long sigh, turns, and walks away into the desert. What God thinks comes tomorrow.
For today, just notice the prayer itself, clumsy and completely sincere.
Your line: in your own words.

how: Alongside set prayers, many traditions make room for personal prayer in a person's own words, and readers of Rumi often point to this story when they talk about it.

o: a person who tends a flock of sheep or goats
a priest who leads a church congregation
a traveling holy man who begs for food

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: tells him to stuff cotton in his mouth
things God has no need of

s: the shepherd was a learned man
he had no learning. he offered God the care he knew how to give.
Moses said God has no need of shoes or milk
he scolded the shepherd for talking to God as if God had a body.
after being scolded, the shepherd argues back
he tears his clothes, sighs, and walks off into the desert.

games.q: you're Moses. you hear a shepherd offering to comb God's hair and rub God's feet. what do you do?
o: scold him for talking about God as if God had a body.
sit down and pray with him.
games.why: Moses scolds him sharply. the shepherd, heartbroken, walks off into the desert. what God thinks comes tomorrow.

practice: Let one or two things you're grateful for today come to mind, and say thank you for them inside, in the plainest words you've got: thanks for the coffee, thanks that the test came back fine.
No borrowed phrases, nothing you'd put in a card. If you pray, you can say it to God; if not, just say it into the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Shepherd. A shepherd prays to comb God's hair and wash God's feet, and the prophet Moses scolds him for it. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: a shepherd. the Persian title of this story is Moses and the shepherd.

carryVoice: Your line: in your own words. Clumsy can still be sincere. The story goes on tomorrow.
